\begin{mdframed}[style=tipbox]
\noindent\textbf{Order-of-magnitude check.}
$I=1\,\mathrm{A}$ for $1\,\mathrm{s}$ means $\Delta Q=1\,\mathrm{C}$.
Since $|e|=1.60\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$, that is about
$6\times 10^{18}$ electrons --- huge numbers of tiny charges.
\end{mdframed}

\subsection{A closed loop is required}
Current in a steady circuit needs a \textbf{complete conducting path}.
Open the switch and the field rearranges so that the net current falls to zero
almost at once --- charge briefly piles at the break until the field inside the
wires vanishes. That is why a single wire dangling from one battery terminal
does nothing useful: there is nowhere for charge to circulate.

Everyday analogy (use carefully): water can flow steadily through a pipe only
if there is a pump and a return path. The pump is like the battery; the flow
rate is like current; the pressure difference is like voltage. The analogy
fails if you push it too far (charge is not a fluid you can ``pour out'' of a
wire), but it helps build intuition for loops and pumps.

%======================================================================
\section{Voltage, e.m.f.\ and potential difference}

input.new_string:
Larger voltage means more energy per coulomb, so a greater tendency to drive
current through a given resistance (and greater hazard).

\subsection{Measuring ideas (preview)}
A voltmeter connected across a cell's terminals on open circuit (no load, or
with a very high-resistance meter) reads approximately the e.m.f.
Connect a load and the terminal reading usually falls --- that drop is the first
clue that the cell has internal resistance (Section~6).

%======================================================================
\section{Resistance and Ohm's law}

\begin{mdframed}[style=tipbox]
\noindent\textbf{DSE use.}
You rarely need the full formal statement. You \emph{do} need the habits:
same $I$ in series; same $V$ in parallel; $\mathcal{E}=IR_{\mathrm{total}}$
for a single-loop ohmic circuit; energy/power accounting around the circuit.
\end{mdframed}

\subsection{Mini worked loop}
Ideal cell $\mathcal{E}=12\,\mathrm{V}$ in series with $R_1=2\,\Omega$ and
$R_2=4\,\Omega$:
\[
I=\frac{12}{2+4}=2\,\mathrm{A},\quad
V_1=4\,\mathrm{V},\quad V_2=8\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
KVL check: $12-4-8=0$. Power check:
$P_{\mathrm{cell}}=VI=24\,\mathrm{W}$ equals
$I^{2}R_1+I^{2}R_2=8+16=24\,\mathrm{W}$.

%======================================================================
\section{Internal resistance}
